title: Estimates
summary: Turn users and actions into QPS and bytes within an order of magnitude.

parts.rule: Turn product assumptions into average and peak request rates, storage growth, and—when relevant—bandwidth. Keep units on every line. A day is about 10^5 seconds, so 1 million events per day is roughly 10 per second. Separate reads from writes, apply a stated peak multiplier, and include multipliers such as feed fanout or replicas only when the chosen path creates them.
parts.why: Numbers distinguish a real bottleneck from an attractive component. Ten writes per second and 10,000 reads per second lead to different storage and caching choices even if both systems have the same user count. The calculation only needs the correct order of magnitude; false precision hides uncertain assumptions rather than improving the design.
parts.example: Assume a photo product has 10 million daily active users. Each loads the feed 8 times per day, so traffic is 80 million feed loads per day. Divide by 86,400 seconds to get about 925 loads per second on average; with a 5× peak, plan for roughly 4,600 per second. If one feed request fetches a page of 20 post references in one query, do not incorrectly multiply database query rate by 20, though image delivery still scales with 20 objects. Suppose 1% of active users upload one photo per day: 100,000 uploads per day, or about 1.2 per second average. At 3 MB per original, new object storage is about 300 GB per day and roughly 110 TB per year before replication or lifecycle deletion. At 500 bytes of metadata per photo, the corresponding database rows grow by only about 50 MB per day. These estimates suggest that object storage and CDN bandwidth deserve attention, while metadata write throughput may fit one primary. They do not yet prove that metadata needs sharding. Write the assumptions beside the arithmetic so an interviewer can change “8 opens” to “20 opens” and see the result update.
parts.use: Estimate early enough to influence the baseline design, then revisit the math when the access path changes. Show average and peak rates separately, distinguish logical operations from downstream fanout, and round to memorable values. Use a range when an input is genuinely uncertain.
parts.refuse: Avoid decimals such as 4,837.2 QPS when every input is a guess. Do not compare a daily total directly with per-second capacity, omit peak traffic for a bursty product, or add shards before showing what one node must handle. Keep storage units and replication factors explicit so MB, GB, and TB cannot silently drift.

body:
Rule. Turn product assumptions into average and peak request rates, storage growth, and—when relevant—bandwidth. Keep units on every line. A day is about 10^5 seconds, so 1 million events per day is roughly 10 per second. Separate reads from writes, apply a stated peak multiplier, and include multipliers such as feed fanout or replicas only when the chosen path creates them.

Why it matters. Numbers distinguish a real bottleneck from an attractive component. Ten writes per second and 10,000 reads per second lead to different storage and caching choices even if both systems have the same user count. The calculation only needs the correct order of magnitude; false precision hides uncertain assumptions rather than improving the design.

Worked example. Assume a photo product has 10 million daily active users. Each loads the feed 8 times per day, so traffic is 80 million feed loads per day. Divide by 86,400 seconds to get about 925 loads per second on average; with a 5× peak, plan for roughly 4,600 per second. If one feed request fetches a page of 20 post references in one query, do not incorrectly multiply database query rate by 20, though image delivery still scales with 20 objects. Suppose 1% of active users upload one photo per day: 100,000 uploads per day, or about 1.2 per second average. At 3 MB per original, new object storage is about 300 GB per day and roughly 110 TB per year before replication or lifecycle deletion. At 500 bytes of metadata per photo, the corresponding database rows grow by only about 50 MB per day. These estimates suggest that object storage and CDN bandwidth deserve attention, while metadata write throughput may fit one primary. They do not yet prove that metadata needs sharding. Write the assumptions beside the arithmetic so an interviewer can change “8 opens” to “20 opens” and see the result update.

[[diagram:back-of-envelope]]

When to use. Estimate early enough to influence the baseline design, then revisit the math when the access path changes. Show average and peak rates separately, distinguish logical operations from downstream fanout, and round to memorable values. Use a range when an input is genuinely uncertain.

When to refuse. Avoid decimals such as 4,837.2 QPS when every input is a guess. Do not compare a daily total directly with per-second capacity, omit peak traffic for a bursty product, or add shards before showing what one node must handle. Keep storage units and replication factors explicit so MB, GB, and TB cannot silently drift.
